reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: One of the eosinophilic gastrointestinal disorders, defined by gastric-predominant eosinophilic infiltration without a secondary cause.

The Klein classification describes disease by depth: mucosal (commonest, causing pain, nausea, bleeding and protein loss), muscular (obstruction and gastric outlet narrowing) and serosal (eosinophilic ascites).
Peripheral eosinophilia is common but not universal, and most patients have an atopic background.
Diagnosis requires gastric biopsies showing excess eosinophils together with exclusion of parasites, drugs, malignancy, hypereosinophilic syndrome and connective tissue disease.
Normal-appearing mucosa does not exclude the diagnosis, so take multiple biopsies.
Serosal disease may present with eosinophil-rich ascites.
Corticosteroids are the mainstay of treatment, with dietary elimination in selected and paediatric cases.
Exclude Strongyloides infection before starting immunosuppression to avoid hyperinfection.
reference.pathophysiology: Eosinophilic gastritis is a Th2-mediated eosinophilic infiltration of the gastric wall driven by interleukin-5, interleukin-13 and eotaxin, frequently in atopic individuals reacting to food antigens. Eosinophil degranulation releases major basic protein and other cytotoxic granule proteins that damage tissue, and the depth of infiltration determines the phenotype: mucosal disease causes malabsorption and protein loss, muscular disease causes obstruction, and serosal disease produces eosinophilic ascites.
additionalDifferentials: Secondary gastric eosinophilia from parasitic infection (Strongyloides, Anisakis)
additionalInvestigations: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy with multiple gastric biopsies and eosinophil quantification
Full blood count with eosinophil count
Cross-sectional imaging for wall thickening or ascites
Ascitic fluid analysis for eosinophils in serosal disease
Screen for hypereosinophilic syndrome and ANCA-associated vasculitis where indicated
redFlags: Gastric outlet obstruction or intractable vomiting
Features suggesting malignancy or systemic vasculitis
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is generally good given corticosteroid responsiveness, but many patients relapse and require maintenance therapy, and a subset follows a chronic remitting-relapsing course.
pitfalls: Starting corticosteroids before excluding Strongyloides, risking hyperinfection
Relying on peripheral eosinophilia, which may be absent
Taking too few biopsies from normal-looking mucosa
Overlooking serosal disease presenting as unexplained eosinophilic ascites

management: Dietary elimination therapy, empirical multi-food or allergy-guided and amino-acid based in severe disease, as a steroid-sparing mainstay
Corticosteroids, including swallowed topical or targeted budesonide, with systemic corticosteroids for extensive disease, to induce remission
Proton pump inhibitors for acid-related symptoms and mucosal healing
Exclude and treat secondary causes such as parasites, drugs and malignancy before diagnosis
Steroid-sparing agents or anti-IL-5 and anti-IL-5-receptor biologics for relapsing or steroid-dependent disease
Manage complications including gastric outlet obstruction from muscular disease, protein loss and eosinophilic ascites
Monitor symptoms and gastric histology with gastroenterology follow-up
